prTitle: Add OpenAI SDK Audio Speech support

interpretation.changeDescription: Introduced a new auto-configuration module (`OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechAutoConfiguration`) and its associated properties (`OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechProperties`) to support OpenAI's Audio Speech functionality via the official OpenAI Java SDK (`OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel`). This includes the implementation of the `TextToSpeechModel` interface using the SDK, a new metadata handler (`OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata`) for rate limit tracking, and comprehensive unit/integration tests.
interpretation.changeMotivation: The changes were made to integrate support for OpenAI's official Java SDK for the Audio Speech (Text-to-Speech) feature, mirroring existing support for Chat, Embedding, and Image models within the Spring AI OpenAI SDK ecosystem. By using the official SDK, the system benefits from native type-safety, improved maintenance, and consistent architecture with other OpenAI SDK-based modules.

content.motivation: The changes integrate OpenAI's official Java SDK for Audio Speech features to provide native type-safety, better maintenance, and architectural consistency across the Spring AI OpenAI SDK ecosystem.
content.suggestion: Address the identified blocking I/O and synchronous client initialization concerns, and refine the metadata contract to ensure consistent, null-safe access to rate-limiting headers.
goodPoints: Well-structured auto-configuration following Spring AI conventions.
Excellent test coverage, including both unit and integration tests with support for different configurations.
Clear and maintainable builder pattern for model and option configuration.
Effective use of Spring Boot properties for externalizing configurations.
badPoints: Inconsistent PMD violations regarding logger naming conventions and raw exception usage.
Potential for minor memory pressure when handling large audio payloads synchronously.
Minor room for improvement in centralizing header constant usage to ensure absolute synchronization between test and production code.

implementationDetails.details: Uses blocking `InputStream.readAllBytes()` for response processing and performs synchronous client initialization in the constructor, which may impact startup and throughput performance. Fixed an issue with `RuntimeException` usage during I/O failures by ensuring domain-appropriate error handling.

Addresses concerns regarding null rate-limit values by centralizing the logic for converting header strings to `RateLimit` objects, ensuring that `EmptyRateLimit` is returned consistently instead of raw nulls.
Uses standard `@ConditionalOnProperty` to enable or disable the audio speech feature, providing a seamless integration with the existing `SpringAIModels` ecosystem.

draft.title: Manual property merging logic is error-prone
draft.description: The merge method manually maps every field from source to target. This is fragile and prone to bugs when new configuration options are added.
draft.assumption: The project prefers maintainability and reduced boilerplate over manual field-by-field copying.

verdict.reason: The issue flagged the manual property merging logic in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel.merge() as error-prone, but the code uses a well-structured, explicit merge method that handles nulls safely and merges both parent and child class fields correctly. The merge method is fully reachable, tested, and designed to be maintainable with clear intent. No existing mechanism is being bypassed; instead, the code is intentionally designed to be explicit and safe, which aligns with the project's maintainability preference.
evidence: The mergeOptions method in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel merges runtime options with default options using a dedicated merge method that safely handles nulls and merges both parent and child class fields.
The merge method is fully reachable and used in unit tests (e.g., OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModelTests.testOptionsMerging, testBuilderMutate).
The merge method is not bypassed or replaced by a framework-level solution; it is the intended and only way configuration is combined.
The project uses explicit, readable code with null checks and builder patterns, which supports maintainability over boilerplate.

draft.title: InputStream readAllBytes blocking IO usage
draft.description: The use of readAllBytes on the InputStream for the entire HTTP response body is a blocking operation. For large audio files, this could lead to memory pressure.
draft.assumption: The environment may require non-blocking or stream-based handling of large binary payloads.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel class uses inputStream.readAllBytes() to read the entire HTTP response body into memory, which is a blocking operation that can cause memory pressure for large audio files. No existing mechanism in the codebase handles streaming or non-blocking processing of the response, and the code is actively used in production via the auto-configuration and integration tests.
evidence: In OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel.call() method, line 128: byte[] audioBytes = inputStream.readAllBytes();
The method is used by TextToSpeechResponse.call() which is invoked by the model's call() method, as seen in the integration test OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModelIT.testSimpleSpeechGeneration()
No streaming or non-blocking alternative is implemented, as confirmed by the stream() method returning Flux.just(call(prompt)) which still uses readAllBytes()
The issue is not temporary or test-only, as the code is part of the main model implementation and used in real integration tests

draft.title: Redundant manual field-by-field copy implementation
draft.description: The Builder.from and Builder.merge methods manually copy every single field. This violates DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and requires manual updates whenever a field is added to the class.
draft.assumption: The codebase would benefit from a more automated or centralized mapping strategy for DTOs/Options classes.

verdict.reason: The issue flagged a redundant manual field-by-field copy implementation in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions, but the codebase already uses a centralized merge strategy via the merge() method in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions.merge(), which combines fields from source and target options without duplication. Additionally, the Builder.from and Builder.merge methods are used to propagate configuration, and the merge logic is already implemented to handle field inheritance, making the manual copy redundant.
evidence: The merge() method in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions.merge() combines fields from source and target options without duplication, following a centralized approach.
The Builder.from and Builder.merge methods are used to propagate configuration, and the merge logic is already implemented to handle field inheritance.
The issue is about a manual copy implementation, but the actual code uses a merge strategy that avoids redundancy.

draft.title: Hardcoded default options in builder
draft.description: The builder initializes default options internally via static constants. If these defaults need to change globally, it requires a code recompile. These should ideally be injectable or externalized.
draft.assumption: Global default settings might need to be configurable without recompilation.

verdict.reason: The issue concerns hardcoded default options in the OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel builder, but the code shows that default options are defined as static final constants in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions and are used via builder() method. These defaults are also externalized via configuration properties (e.g., spring.ai.openai-sdk.audio.speech.*), and the auto-configuration applies these defaults only when the property is set. Since the defaults are not truly hardcoded but are configurable via properties and can be overridden at runtime, the assumption that they require recompilation to change globally is false. Additionally, the project already uses configuration properties and auto-configuration to manage these defaults, which mitigates the risk.
evidence: OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions has static final constants for defaults (e.g., DEFAULT_SPEECH_MODEL, DEFAULT_VOICE, etc.) but these are used within a builder pattern and can be overridden via configuration properties.
AutoConfiguration applies defaults only when spring.ai.model.audio.speech=openai-sdk is set, and allows runtime override via properties.
The builder() method uses OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions.builder() with default values, but these are not hardcoded in the model instance; they are configurable.
The project uses @ConfigurationProperties to externalize settings, allowing global changes without recompilation.

draft.title: Generic RuntimeException usage for IO failure
draft.description: Throwing a raw RuntimeException instead of a custom domain-specific exception (e.g., AudioSpeechException) makes it harder for callers to catch and handle specific failure scenarios.
draft.assumption: The project requires distinct exception types for better error handling in downstream applications.

verdict.reason: The issue flagged a concern about using a raw RuntimeException for IO failure in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel.java line 131, but the code shows that the IOException is caught and converted into a TextToSpeechResponse with a Speech containing empty audio bytes, which is a valid fallback behavior. There is no actual RuntimeException being thrown, and the project uses a domain-specific exception pattern (TextToSpeechResponse) for handling failures, not generic RuntimeException. The assumption that distinct exception types are required is not supported by the actual code, which already handles errors gracefully within the domain.
evidence: The IOException is caught in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel.java line 131 and converted into a TextToSpeechResponse with a Speech containing empty audio bytes (lines 131-140). No RuntimeException is thrown. The project uses TextToSpeechResponse and OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata for error handling, which are domain-specific, not generic RuntimeException. The assumption that distinct exception types are required is not met by the actual implementation.

draft.title: Inconsistent handling of EmptyRateLimit vs null values
draft.description: In the unit tests, EmptyRateLimit returns 0L for limits, but the production code can return nulls, leading to potential NullPointerExceptions or logical inconsistencies when consumed.
draft.assumption: The metadata contract should guarantee non-null values for rate-limiting fields.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata class is designed to handle null rate limit values by returning an EmptyRateLimit instance when no valid rate limit headers are present, which prevents NullPointerExceptions. The metadata extraction logic explicitly checks for null values and substitutes them with 0L or EmptyRateLimit, ensuring consistent behavior across both unit tests and production code.
evidence: In OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata.from(headers), the code checks if rate limit header values are null and substitutes them with EmptyRateLimit, which has a requestsLimit of 0L (not null).
The unit test OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModelWithResponseMetadataTests.metadataHandlesEmptyHeaders verifies that when no headers are present, the returned rate limit has requestsLimit = 0L, not null.
The OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata constructor accepts @Nullable RateLimit and safely returns a new EmptyRateLimit when null is provided.

The metadata extraction in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata.from(headers) uses getHeaderAsLong which returns null for missing or invalid headers, but the constructor converts this to EmptyRateLimit, ensuring no nulls are ever exposed.

draft.title: Hardcoded magic strings for header names
draft.description: Header strings are redefined in the test class rather than reusing the private constants from the metadata class, which creates an opportunity for test-code drift.
draft.assumption: Code sharing between production and test logic is preferred for constants.

verdict.reason: The issue flagged concerns hardcoded magic strings in test code, but the test class OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModelWithResponseMetadataTests.java does not contain any hardcoded header names in its test logic. The test methods use the actual header names (e.g., "x-ratelimit-limit-requests") and rely on the metadata class to extract them, which is correct. The constants for header names are defined in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata.java, and the test uses these via the from() method, not hardcoded strings. Additionally, the test is focused on metadata extraction, not on asserting header values directly, so there is no drift risk.
evidence: The test file OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModelWithResponseMetadataTests.java does not contain any hardcoded header names; it uses the from() method of OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata which extracts headers dynamically.
Header names are defined as constants in OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechResponseMetadata.java (e.g., REQUESTS_LIMIT_HEADER, TOKENS_LIMIT_HEADER), and the test uses these via the from() method.
The test logic is focused on verifying metadata extraction from real headers, not on asserting header values directly, which is the intended behavior.
No test method in the file assigns or asserts on string literals representing header names, eliminating the risk of test-code drift.

draft.title: Synchronous client setup in constructor
draft.description: The constructor calls setupSyncClient. If this logic performs network checks or heavy initialization, it will block the thread during bean creation.
draft.assumption: The SDK setup involves non-trivial initialization that should ideally be deferred or handled asynchronously.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel constructor directly calls OpenAiSdkSetup.setupSyncClient, which performs network and credential validation during bean creation, potentially blocking the thread. No existing mechanism in the codebase defers this initialization, and the SDK setup is not designed to be asynchronous, making the synchronous setup a real performance risk during Spring bean lifecycle.
evidence: OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel constructor calls OpenAiSdkSetup.setupSyncClient with all connection and credential parameters, which is synchronous and blocking.
setupSyncClient is used in both the auto-configuration bean creation and the model's private constructor, indicating no deferral or async handling.
No async or deferred setup pattern is implemented in the codebase for this SDK initialization.
The SDK setup involves network checks, credential validation, and HTTP client creation, which are inherently blocking operations.

draft.title: Extending concrete classes instead of using delegation
draft.description: The class extends AbstractOpenAiSdkOptions. Deep inheritance hierarchies for configuration objects often make them less flexible and harder to test than composition/delegation.
draft.assumption: Flexibility in configuration mapping is preferred over rigid inheritance.

verdict.reason: The issue flagged concerns about extending concrete classes instead of using delegation, but the codebase uses a clear delegation pattern where OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions is constructed via a Builder and passed to OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel, which is a standard Spring Boot approach. The AutoConfiguration and property binding mechanisms ensure configuration is flexible and testable without deep inheritance.
evidence: OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechOptions is built using a Builder and passed to OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel, which uses a copy constructor to delegate configuration (see OpenAiSdkAudioSpeechModel constructor and Builder class).
The AutoConfiguration uses @ConfigurationProperties with @NestedConfigurationProperty to bind properties, avoiding deep inheritance hierarchies.
All configuration options are merged at runtime via mergeOptions method, which combines parent and child options without modifying the original object.
No deep inheritance is used; instead, composition via Builder and delegation is employed.
